title: Why Your Brain Deletes Most of What You See
summary: Your eyes take in far more information than your conscious mind ever processes. This Short explains the attentional bottleneck and change blindness in under 30 seconds.
hook: You just missed something huge... and your brain is the reason.
narration: Right now your eyes are taking in millions of bits of information. But your conscious mind only processes a tiny fraction. Scientists call this the attentional bottleneck. In classic change-blindness experiments, people fail to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through a scene. Your brain is not a camera. It is a ruthless editor. It keeps what it thinks matters and throws the rest away. That is why you can look straight at something and still not see it.

title: The Number That Breaks Infinity
summary: Hilbert’s Hotel shows how infinity can still have empty rooms even when every room is full. A clean visual explanation of countable infinity.
hook: A hotel with infinite rooms is completely full... yet it still has space for more guests.
narration: Imagine a hotel with infinitely many rooms, and every single room is occupied. A new guest arrives. Is the hotel full? Not quite. The manager asks the guest in room 1 to move to room 2, the guest in room 2 to move to room 3, and so on. Suddenly room 1 is free. This is Hilbert’s Hotel, a thought experiment that shows countable infinity can still absorb more. Infinity is not a number. It is a different kind of size.

title: Why Time Moves Slower When You Move Faster
summary: Special relativity time dilation explained in plain language with a clear visual of clocks running at different rates.
hook: The faster you move, the slower time passes for you. This is not science fiction.
narration: According to Einstein’s special relativity, time is not absolute. If you travel close to the speed of light, your clock runs slower compared to someone standing still. This is called time dilation. GPS satellites have to correct for it every day or their positioning would drift. The effect is tiny at everyday speeds, but it is real, measured, and built into the technology you use.

title: The Place on Earth Where Gravity Is Weakest
summary: Gravity is not the same everywhere. There is a measurable difference between the poles and the equator, and even smaller local anomalies.
hook: Gravity is weaker in some places on Earth than others. Here is why.
narration: You weigh slightly less at the equator than at the poles. Two reasons: Earth is spinning, so centrifugal force pulls you outward, and Earth is not a perfect sphere — it bulges at the equator. There are also local gravity anomalies caused by dense rock or mountain ranges. These differences are tiny, but satellites measure them precisely. Gravity is not a fixed number. It is a field that varies.

title: Why Hot Water Can Freeze Faster Than Cold Water
summary: The Mpemba effect is a real observed phenomenon where, under certain conditions, hotter water freezes faster than colder water.
hook: Hot water can freeze faster than cold water. Scientists still debate exactly why.
narration: In some conditions, hot water freezes faster than cold water. This is called the Mpemba effect, named after a Tanzanian student who noticed it. Possible explanations include evaporation reducing the mass, differences in convection currents, dissolved gases, and supercooling. The effect is real but does not always happen. It depends on the container, the starting temperatures, and the environment. Nature still has surprises.

title: The Tiny Animal That Can Survive Outer Space
summary: Tardigrades (water bears) can survive extreme radiation, vacuum, and dehydration. Some have been exposed to open space and lived.
hook: There is an animal that has survived the vacuum of outer space.
narration: Tardigrades, also called water bears, are microscopic animals that can survive conditions that would kill almost anything else. They can dry out completely, withstand extreme radiation, and endure the vacuum of space. In experiments, tardigrades have been exposed to open space and later revived. They enter a state called cryptobiosis. When conditions improve, they rehydrate and continue living. They are one of the toughest forms of life we know.

title: Why Black Holes Are Not Black
summary: Black holes emit Hawking radiation and can be detected by their influence on surrounding matter and light.
hook: Black holes are not completely black. Here is what we actually see.
narration: A black hole itself does not emit light from inside the event horizon. But that does not mean it is invisible. Matter swirling around it forms an accretion disk that can glow brighter than entire galaxies. In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope captured the shadow of a black hole. Stephen Hawking also predicted that black holes slowly emit radiation and can eventually evaporate. We detect black holes by how they bend light and disrupt nearby stars and gas.

title: The Paradox That Breaks Your Intuition About Probability
summary: The Monty Hall problem shows that switching doors doubles your chance of winning. A classic probability counter-intuitive result.
hook: You should almost always switch doors. The math is clear.
narration: There are three doors. Behind one is a car, behind the others are goats. You pick a door. The host, who knows what is behind the doors, opens another door that has a goat. Should you stay or switch? Switching gives you a two-thirds chance of winning. Staying leaves you with one-third. Most people feel it should be fifty-fifty. It is not. This is the Monty Hall problem, and it has been verified both mathematically and by simulation.
